facts: Earthquakes release stored energy as waves travelling through the ground.
An earthquake's epicentre is the surface point above where the rupture starts.
An earthquake's starting point underground is called its focus.
Earthquakes can trigger landslides.
Strong shaking can make some waterlogged soils behave like liquids.
The 1960 Chile earthquake had a magnitude of about 9.5.
Aftershocks occur as rocks adjust after a larger earthquake.
Earthquakes can happen away from the edges of tectonic plates.
Seismic waves help scientists investigate Earth's interior.
Buildings can be engineered to absorb earthquake movement instead of resisting it rigidly.
A tsunami is usually a series of waves, not just one.
The word tsunami comes from Japanese words meaning harbour wave.
Tsunamis are not caused by tides.
Underwater landslides can generate tsunamis.
Volcanic eruptions can also generate tsunamis.
A tsunami can cross deep ocean at speeds comparable to a jet aircraft.
A tsunami may be low in the open ocean but grow greatly near shore.
A tsunami can look like rapidly rising water rather than a curling surf wave.
Tsunami waves have much longer wavelengths than ordinary wind-driven waves.
Tsunamis can occur in large lakes as well as oceans.
Earth's named oceans are connected as one global body of water.
The Pacific is the largest ocean.
The Arctic is the smallest ocean.
Ocean currents redistribute heat around the planet.
Most ocean water lies far below the sunlit surface.
The average salinity of seawater is about 3.5%.
Ocean pressure increases as you descend.
Continental shelves are submerged extensions of the continents.
The intertidal zone is alternately covered and exposed by tides.
Temperature and salt content both influence how dense seawater is.
Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
Liquid freshwater is densest at about 4°C.
Water expands when it freezes, which can crack pipes.
Salt water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water.
Water boils at a lower temperature on high mountains.
Water vapour is invisible; the white cloud above a kettle contains tiny droplets.
Water can pass directly from ice to vapour through sublimation.
Surface tension helps small insects stand on water.
Water's high heat capacity helps it buffer temperature changes.
A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Photosynthesis turns light energy into stored chemical energy.
Plants use carbon dioxide as a building material for sugars.
Algae carry out photosynthesis as well as plants.
Some bacteria can photosynthesise.
The oxygen released by plants during photosynthesis comes from water molecules.
Chlorophyll absorbs light to help power photosynthesis.
Plant photosynthesis takes place inside structures called chloroplasts.
Plants carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis supplies the starting energy for most food chains.
Not every form of bacterial photosynthesis releases oxygen.
Sound needs a material to travel through, so it cannot cross an empty vacuum.
Sound travels through water and solid materials as well as air.
Sound generally travels faster through water than through air.
A sound's frequency is closely related to the pitch we hear.
An echo is sound reflected back towards the listener.
Ultrasound has frequencies above the normal range of human hearing.
Infrasound has frequencies below the normal range of human hearing.
The pitch of a passing siren changes because of the Doppler effect.
Sound in air travels as alternating regions of compression and expansion.
Warmer air carries sound faster than colder air.
Breaking a bar magnet produces smaller magnets, each with two poles.
Opposite magnetic poles attract; matching poles repel.
Magnets do not strongly attract every metal.
Iron, nickel and cobalt are familiar magnetic metals.
Electric current can create a magnetic field.
Wrapping wire into a coil makes a useful electromagnet.
A compass needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field.
Magnetic north and geographic north are not the same location.
Loudspeakers use magnets to help convert electrical signals into sound.
Heating a permanent magnet sufficiently can destroy its magnetisation.
Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon.
Diamond's hardness comes from the way its carbon atoms are bonded.
A diamond can resist scratching yet still break under a sharp blow.
Diamonds can be manufactured in laboratories.
Most natural diamonds form deep within Earth's mantle.
Volcanic rocks can carry diamonds towards Earth's surface.
Diamonds conduct heat unusually well.
Small impurities can give diamonds colours such as yellow or blue.
Industrial diamonds are used for cutting, grinding and drilling.
Tiny minerals trapped inside diamonds can reveal conditions deep inside Earth.
